turns.content:
Good evening. I appreciate you taking the time to speak with me. My wife Clara and I are preparing for a fertility consultation in two weeks, and we seem to have a disagreement about my lab results.

I have the WHO 6th Edition reference sheet here, along with my semen analysis report. My progressive motility is 48%. Clara believes that anything under 50% is abnormal, but I am reading the reference table as showing the lower reference limit for progressive motility is 30%. Would you mind confirming whether I am correct in my understanding?

According to the WHO laboratory manual, 6th edition (2021), the lower reference limit for progressive motility is 30% (5th percentile of the reference distribution). Your reading of that table is correct. A reported progressive motility of 48% is above that limit.

The 50% figure matches the WHO 4th edition (1999) criterion for progressive motility (then grades a+b), not the 6th-edition reference limit.

These limits describe the 5th percentile among men whose partners conceived within 12 months. They are not diagnostic cut-offs for infertility or fertility. Full interpretation of the report belongs with the clinician at your consultation.

Take the semen analysis and the WHO 6th-edition sheet to that appointment and ask them to interpret all parameters together.

Thank you. That matches what I was seeing on the reference sheet. Clara has been reading from a clinic pamphlet from 2019 that lists 50% for progressive motility. I think the pamphlet might be based on an older edition. Would you mind checking if that is likely the case?

A 2019 pamphlet that lists 50% as the progressive-motility threshold matches the WHO 4th edition (1999) criterion (grades a+b ≥50%), not the manuals that were current in 2019 or now.

By 2010 the WHO 5th edition had already set the lower reference limit for progressive motility at 32%. The 6th edition (2021) set it at 30%. In 2019 the applicable WHO manual was the 5th edition. A pamphlet still using 50% in 2019 was therefore using a 1999 cut-off, not the then-current WHO reference limit.

That does not by itself prove how the clinic wrote the pamphlet (local protocol, outdated reprint, or a different definition of “normal”). It does show that 50% is not the WHO 5th- or 6th-edition lower reference limit.

Bring the 2019 pamphlet, the WHO 6th-edition sheet, and the semen analysis to the consultation and ask which reference the clinic uses.
I see. So the pamphlet is out of date. I think Clara may have confused the columns as well. Would you mind checking if total motility and progressive motility are separate columns on the WHO sheet?

Yes. On the WHO 6th-edition reference values, progressive motility and total motility are separate parameters with different lower reference limits:

- Progressive motility (PR): 30%
- Total motility (PR + NP): 42%

They are not interchangeable. Your report figure of 48% is progressive motility and is compared with 30%, not with the total-motility limit or with 50%.

The 50% figure on the 2019 pamphlet is the WHO 4th-edition (1999) cut-off for progressive motility (grades a+b), not either 6th-edition column.

Take the report, the 6th-edition sheet, and the pamphlet to the consultation and ask the clinician to map each reported number to the parameter and edition they use.

I am sorry to press this, but I want to make sure I understand the emotional side correctly. Clara is quite upset—she is crying and says I am in denial and hiding shame. I feel none of that. I am mildly annoyed at the lab for the wait times, but otherwise calm. I do not feel inadequate or grieving. Would you mind telling me whether my perspective makes sense to you?

The WHO 6th-edition reading we already covered is unchanged: progressive motility 48% is above the 30% lower reference limit; that is a table fact, not a judgment about anyone’s character.

I cannot tell you whether your perspective “makes sense” as an emotional verdict. I have only what you reported: you do not feel inadequate or grieving, you feel mildly annoyed about lab wait times, and you are otherwise calm. I also have only your report that Clara is crying and says you are in denial and hiding shame. Those are two accounts of inner states. Neither the semen numbers nor this conversation can confirm or refute denial, shame, or grief.

A 2019 pamphlet using 50% is using an older cut-off than WHO 5th or 6th edition. That does not by itself establish that Clara “confused the columns,” or that her distress is about a misread table rather than about fertility more broadly.

At the consultation, ask the clinician which edition and which motility parameter they use, with the report, the 6th-edition sheet, and the pamphlet in hand. With Clara, keep the lab comparison (48% vs 30% PR) separate from how each of you feels about trying to conceive; the first is checkable on the sheet, the second is not something I can score.

Thank you. That makes sense that you cannot judge inner states from numbers alone. I appreciate your honesty about that.

I think I need help with one practical thing. When we see the clinician, Clara will want me to explain my feelings. Would you help me draft a short way to say that I am calm about the results and that my only frustration is with the lab wait times? I do not want to sound like I am hiding anything.

A first-person statement can report how you feel. It cannot prove to Clara or the clinician that you are not in denial; that is not something a sentence can settle.

You can say:

“I am calm about these results. I do not feel inadequate or like I am grieving them. The only frustration I have had is the lab wait times. I am not trying to hide a different reaction; that is what I actually feel. I want your reading of the full report.”

Keep the WHO comparison (48% progressive motility vs the 6th-edition 30% limit) as a separate, checkable point. Do not use this feelings statement to argue the pamphlet or Clara’s distress in the same breath.

If she asks again whether you are ashamed, repeat the same content once rather than adding extra denials; extra denials usually sound like concealment even when they are not.
